summary: This informational memo gives application-specific requirements for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) when used in Wavelength Switched Optical Networks. Lightpath provisioning needs Routing and Wavelength Assignment, and this lists what PCEP must support for it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7449 explains what a path computation element needs to hear before it can set up a lightpath, which is a route through an optical network. The route is only half the answer: the element must also say which wavelength of light to use on each fibre, and that depends on the equipment at the ends and on what is already there. The document lists what the request must carry and what the reply must say.

questions: what is routing and wavelength assignment
subtitle: What a path computation element has to be told to place an optical path and pick its wavelength.

tldr.problem: In an optical network a path is not enough. The path computation element must also choose a wavelength for every link, and that choice is constrained by what the equipment can do and by what is already in the fibre.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7449 sets out requirements for the path computation protocol in this setting: how the request says whether it wants routing only or routing with wavelength assignment, what wavelength information it carries, how the answer reports what was assigned or why nothing could be assigned, and how a path can be re-optimised later.
tldr.outcome: The document covers the combined process, where one element both chooses the path and assigns the wavelengths. The other two ways of splitting the work are left to the Generalized MPLS extensions of the protocol.

today: RFC 7449 is an Informational RFC published in February 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It is a set of requirements: the document expects a matching solution document to define the protocol extensions and to say what is added to the management module.

sections.title: What a Wavelength Switched Optical Network Is
sections.content:
The path computation element architecture describes a component that computes label switched paths for packet networks at the request of a client. The client may be any network component, and in the case of an optical network it may be an optical switching element inside a wavelength division multiplexing network. The element itself may sit anywhere: inside an optical switch, in a network management system or operational support system, or on its own server. The communication protocol between client and element may also be used between cooperating elements, and the common requirements for that protocol are set out separately, with application-specific requirements left to other documents. This one covers the case of path computation in wavelength switched optical networks, where the switching is done selectively according to the wavelength of the optical signal.

The path through such a network is called a lightpath. It may cross several fibre links, and a wavelength should be assigned for each of them. A transparent optical network is built from devices that can switch but cannot convert one wavelength into another, so a lightpath there runs on the same wavelength across every fibre it crosses, which is called the wavelength-continuity constraint. Two lightpaths that share a fibre link cannot be given the same wavelength, because the signals would interfere with each other. The document leaves out advanced multiplexing such as polarization-based multiplexing, because the physical layer aspects are not standardised, which makes choosing the right wavelength an essential part of optical path computation.

Where a node can convert wavelengths, the continuity constraint can be relaxed and a lightpath may use different wavelengths on different links. Converters may be limited for cost reasons, and the number of wavelengths a fibre can carry is also limited, and a network may mix nodes with no conversion, limited conversion and full conversion. Wavelength assignment is therefore an extra constraint that every lightpath computation has to take into account.
sections.plainLanguage: An optical network sends light down fibres, and each fibre carries several wavelengths at once, each on its own signal. A lightpath is a route through the network, and it needs one wavelength per fibre. Where the equipment cannot change the wavelength along the way, the same wavelength must be used on every fibre, and no two lightpaths on the same fibre may use the same wavelength.

sections.title: Three Ways to Route and Assign Wavelengths
sections.content:
Three alternative process architectures for routing and wavelength assignment were set out earlier, and they shape the requirements in this document. In the combined process, path selection and wavelength assignment are done together as a single process. In routing separate from wavelength assignment, the routing process produces one or more candidate paths and the wavelength assignment process then makes the final choice of path and of wavelengths; the requirements for a client talking to one element that routes and another that assigns wavelengths are not addressed here. In routing with distributed wavelength assignment, a standard path computation happens without any knowledge of wavelength availability, and the wavelengths are then assigned along that path in a distributed way through signalling. That last case is a particular form of the separate approach, is expected to be covered by the Generalized MPLS extensions of the communication protocol, and raises no new requirements specific to optical networks.

The requirements in this document are written against the combined process. In that architecture, one element offers both functions, the routing and the wavelength assignment, and the client talks to it over the path computation protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to organise the work. One element can choose the route and the wavelengths together. Two elements can split the job, one choosing routes and one choosing wavelengths. Or a route can be chosen without any knowledge of wavelengths and the wavelengths assigned later as the path is set up. The document takes the first of these as its model.

sections.title: What the Request and the Reply Must Carry
sections.content:
A request may carry the path computation type, which is either routing with wavelength assignment or routing only. The distinction is needed so that the combined process can be told apart from the distributed wavelength assignment option, where wavelengths are assigned at each node along the route as it is set up.

When the request is for routing with wavelength assignment, it must also carry the wavelength assignment options, and at least two should be supported: explicit label control, and a set of recommended labels for each hop, from which the client can pick one according to local policy. The second of these can also be used in the other two process models. The reply to such a request must include the wavelengths assigned to the path and say which of the two label assignment options was applied. Where no valid path is found, the reply must say why, for example that the network is disconnected or that no wavelength was found, and the wavelength case can have sub-cases such as the continuity constraint not being met or an unsupported forward error correction or modulation type.

Requests for routing only can already be sent in bulk by the protocol, and the same is required for routing with wavelength assignment: a request must be able to ask for a number of simultaneous computations, and the reply must give the path and the assigned wavelength for each of them.

Reoptimization is also covered. A reoptimization request must provide both the path and the current wavelength, and may say whether the wavelength should be kept while the path may change, whether the path should be kept while the wavelength may change, or whether both may change. The reply must give the reoptimized path and wavelengths even when the request asked for one of them to stay the same, and if no new path is found it must say why, in the same terms as before.
sections.plainLanguage: The request has to say whether it wants a route only or a route with wavelengths. If it wants wavelengths, it must also say how the wavelengths should be chosen: either fixed by the element, or as a list of suggestions the client can pick from. The reply has to state the wavelengths it used and say which method it used, and if it could not find a path it has to say whether the problem was the network or the wavelengths.

sections.title: Wavelength Ranges, Preferences and Signal Types
sections.content:
The client must be allowed to restrict which wavelengths may be used. The restriction might come from the tuning range of a laser transmitter, from the capability of some other optical element, or from a policy decision. The client is not obliged to supply any restriction.

Where the network has wavelength conversion, for example at sparse regenerators, the request should be able to say whether a single continuous wavelength is wanted anyway, so that the client can set the precedence of the continuity constraint even where it could be relaxed. The request may also state a preference for how the wavelengths are picked, such as random, descending or ascending order, and the reply should follow that preference unless it conflicts with the operator's policy. A request for two or more paths must allow the client to constrain them to the same wavelengths, which is what protection with a single transponder needs, such as a pair of link-disjoint paths for 1+1 protection.

Signal processing is the other constraint that matters. The signal type of an end-to-end optical path must match at the source and the destination, so the client must be able to state the signal type at the endpoints. At a minimum, a modulation type list and a forward error correction type list should be supported, and the client must also be able to say whether transit modification of those capabilities is acceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: Three more things shape the answer. The client can rule out wavelengths that its hardware cannot produce or that policy forbids. It can ask for one continuous wavelength even where the network could change it, and can express a preference for how the wavelengths are picked. And it must be able to say what kind of signal it needs at each end, because the signal has to be the same at both ends of the path.

sections.title: Running It in Practice
sections.content:
Manageability has to cover a few practical points. A client should be able to configure the ability to send a request for routing with wavelength assignment. On the element's side, the session parameters should include support for that kind of request and the maximum number of bulk path requests that may be associated with it in one request message. These parameters may be set as defaults for any session the speaker takes part in, or for a specific session with a given peer or a specific group of sessions with a given group of peers.

The document defines no new management information module, because it only covers requirements; the matching solution document will list what should be added to the path computation element's management module. It defines no new liveness detection or monitoring mechanisms beyond those already in the protocol, and no new verification requirements beyond those already there. If the discovery mechanisms were extended for technology-specific capabilities, advertising the ability to compute optical paths should be considered. And no new network operation requirements are implied.
sections.plainLanguage: The operational side is mostly left to the existing protocol. The document adds two things an operator can configure: whether a client may send these requests at all, and how many such requests may be sent in one message. It also notes that if the protocol's discovery mechanism is ever extended to advertise what an element can do, this ability should be one of the things advertised.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document requires no change to the security model of the path computation protocol. It does note, however, that the extra information exchanged to solve the wavelength assignment problem discloses facts about the network's capabilities that an operator may want to keep private, and that securing this information should be considered. A solution that meets these requirements has to check that the existing security mechanisms of the protocol adequately protect the additional network capabilities, and must include new mechanisms where they do not.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not change the protocol's security rules, but it points out that telling the element what wavelengths are available, and what the equipment can do, reveals more about the network than before. An operator who wants that kept private needs the exchange to be protected.

viz.caption: THE THREE WAYS TO ASK FOR A PATH TO BE REOPTIMIZED
WHAT THE REPLY HAS TO SAY

items.title: The wavelengths assigned
items.text: Which wavelength was chosen for each link of the path.

items.title: The method used
items.text: Whether the wavelengths came from explicit label control or from a set of suggestions.

items.title: Why nothing could be assigned
items.text: The network is disconnected, no wavelength was found, or both.

items.title: Which wavelength failed
items.text: Continuity could not be met, or the signal type was not supported.

items.title: Every path in a bulk request
items.text: The path and the assigned wavelength for each request that was sent.

items.title: The reoptimized result
items.text: The path and the wavelengths, even if one of them was asked to stay the same.
